learn.hook: Your morning cup of chai needs a tea farmer in Assam, a truck driver, a shopkeeper and a price you can afford. Who studies how all these people and places are linked? Social scientists do!
points: Social science is the careful, systematic study of human society: how people live together, work, make rules, use resources and change over time.
In Classes 9 and 10 it is studied through four main disciplines: History, Geography, Political Science and Economics.
History studies the human past and how things changed; Geography studies places, location and how people and the environment affect each other.
Political Science studies governance, institutions, power and how public decisions are made; Economics studies how people make choices about limited resources.
Social science depends on evidence. A good social scientist separates personal opinion from claims that can be supported by facts.

example.q: Think it through: A new bus route starts in your town. Which question would each social science discipline ask about it?
steps: Geography: Which places and villages does the route connect, and why was this road chosen?
Economics: How much does a ticket cost, and who can now reach jobs or markets more cheaply?
Political Science: Who decided to start the route, and how did the local government make the decision?
History: How did people of this town travel twenty or fifty years ago, and what has changed?
example.answer: Each discipline looks at the same event from a different angle: place, money and choices, decision-making, and change over time.

learn.reallife: When you read a newspaper story about floods, elections, prices of onions or an old fort being restored, you are reading social science in action.

topics.title: How we know about the past: sources and evidence

learn.hook: A coin found in a farmer's field in Andhra Pradesh can tell us which king ruled, what language was used and how far traders travelled. Clues like this are a historian's treasure.
points: Historians use sources: things from the past that give evidence about it.
Archaeological sources are material remains such as tools, pottery, beads, buildings, terracotta figurines and fossils, found by careful excavation.
Epigraphic sources are inscriptions carved or written on hard surfaces such as rock, pillars or copper plates; numismatic sources are coins.
Written (literary) sources include texts such as the Arthashastra, credited to Kautilya; oral traditions, songs and family records (genealogies) also preserve memory of the past.
Every source must be checked. Historians compare sources and ask who made them and why. Scientific methods such as carbon-14 dating help find the age of ancient remains.

example.q: Think it through: An old copper plate records a king giving land to a village temple. What can a historian learn from it, and what should she be careful about?
steps: It is an epigraphic source, because the record is engraved on metal.
It can show the king's name, the language and script used, place names and how land was granted.
It was written on the king's orders, so it may praise the king more than ordinary people would.
She should compare it with other sources such as coins, other inscriptions and excavated remains.
example.answer: It gives useful evidence about rulers, language and land grants, but it must be checked against other sources because it shows the ruler's point of view.

topics.title: How history, geography, civics and economics connect

learn.hook: When the monsoon fails in a village in Marathwada, crops dry up, families lose income, the government plans relief and some people migrate. One drought, four subjects!
points: Real problems rarely fit into a single subject. Studying them using several disciplines together is called an interdisciplinary approach.
Geography gives the spatial perspective: where something happens and why that location matters, using maps, globes, atlases and GIS.
Economics shows effects on incomes, prices and jobs; Political Science shows how governments and local bodies such as panchayats respond.
History shows how a place or problem has changed over time, for example how settlements grew after farming and the taming of animals began.

Ideas from India's past, such as vasudhaiva kutumbakam ('the world is one family'), remind us that societies everywhere are connected. Sustainable development means meeting today's needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

example.q: Think it through: India has a long coastline. How can this one geographical fact connect to history and economics?
steps: Geography: a long coastline gives many natural harbours and access to the sea.
History: for thousands of years ships from Indian ports traded with distant lands, carrying goods and ideas.
Economics: ports create jobs in fishing, shipping and trade, and goods can be exchanged with other countries.
So a fact about location helps explain past events and present livelihoods.
example.answer: The coastline (geography) made sea trade possible in the past (history) and supports jobs and trade today (economics).

learn.reallife: Planning a new metro line in a city needs maps (geography), budgets (economics), government approval (political science) and knowledge of old buildings in the way (history).

topics.title: Early humans: from hunter-gatherers to the first artists

learn.hook: Thousands of years ago, someone in a rock shelter in Madhya Pradesh dipped a finger in red colour and painted a running animal. Those paintings at Bhimbetka still survive!
points: Humans evolved over a very long time. Several human species once existed, such as Homo erectus and the Neanderthals, but Homo sapiens (modern humans) is the only human species living today.
Homo erectus made handaxes and cleavers and was among the early humans to spread out of Africa into Asia and Europe. Over time, skulls became larger and rounder and jaws and teeth became smaller.
Palaeolithic (Old Stone Age) people were hunter-gatherers: they hunted animals, gathered wild plants, moved in search of food and water, and lived in caves, rock shelters or temporary camps.
In the Mesolithic (Middle Stone Age), people used microliths: tiny stone tools often fitted into wooden or bone handles to make arrows, spears and sickles.

Before writing, people communicated through speech, gestures, body decoration, engravings and paintings. The rock shelters of Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, preserve such early art.

example.q: Think it through: Archaeologists find a cave with ash, animal bones and many small stone blades. What can they infer about the people who lived there?
steps: Ash suggests the people used fire, for warmth, light, cooking or keeping animals away.
Animal bones suggest they hunted animals for food.
Small stone blades (microliths) suggest they made fine tools, probably fixed into handles.
Since there are no farm tools or houses, they were probably hunter-gatherers who used the cave as a shelter.
example.answer: They were probably Stone Age hunter-gatherers who used fire, hunted animals and made microlith tools.

topics.title: The Neolithic revolution: farming and settled life

learn.hook: Imagine never having to chase your dinner again! When people learned to grow wheat and barley and keep goats, life changed forever.
points: The Neolithic (New Stone Age) brought a great change called the Neolithic revolution: people began growing crops and taming (domesticating) animals such as cattle, sheep and goats.
Farming meant people stayed near their fields, so they built permanent houses and villages. They used polished stone tools, made pottery to store grain and began weaving cloth.
Mehrgarh, in present-day Balochistan (Pakistan), is one of the earliest farming villages in South Asia. People there grew wheat and barley, kept animals and built mud-brick houses and storage rooms.

Extra food (surplus) could be stored, so some people could become potters, weavers or other specialists. Settled life also brought new problems such as crop failure and the need to protect stored grain.
In the Chalcolithic (Copper-Stone) age, people used copper along with stone. Later, people learned to make bronze, a mixture of copper and tin, which gave the Bronze Age its name.

example.q: Think it through: Why did farming lead people to make pottery?
steps: Farmers harvested more grain than they could eat at once.
The surplus had to be stored safely away from damp, insects and rats.
Clay pots could store grain, water and oil, and could also be used for cooking.
Since people now stayed in one place, heavy pots were not a burden to carry around.
example.answer: Settled farmers needed containers to store and cook their surplus food, so pottery became important.

learn.reallife: The earthen matka that keeps water cool in many Indian homes in summer is part of a pottery tradition that began with the first farmers.

learn.hook: More than 4,000 years ago, cities in north-western India had straight streets, covered drains and standard weights. Town planners today still admire them!
points: The Harappan civilisation, also called the Indus or Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation, was a Bronze Age civilisation. Its mature, urban phase is dated to about 2600-1900 BCE.
Important sites include Harappa and Mohenjo-daro (now in Pakistan), and Dholavira and Lothal (Gujarat), Kalibangan (Rajasthan) and Rakhigarhi (Haryana) in India.

Cities were planned with streets meeting at right angles, houses of baked bricks of standard proportions and covered drains. Mohenjo-daro had the Great Bath, Dholavira had large water reservoirs and Lothal had a dockyard.

Harappans used standard cubical stone weights. Smaller weights followed a doubling pattern (1, 2, 4, 8, 16...) and larger ones used multiples of ten. Kalibangan shows a ploughed field with criss-cross furrows.
They traded with Mesopotamia, whose records probably called the region 'Meluhha'. The Harappan script, found on seals and pots, has not yet been deciphered.

example.q: Think it through: Why have scholars still not been able to read the Harappan script?
steps: Most inscriptions are very short, often only a few signs on a seal.
No bilingual inscription has been found, like the Rosetta Stone that gave the same text in known and unknown scripts.
We do not know for certain which language the Harappans spoke.
Without longer texts or a key, scholars cannot confidently match signs to sounds or words.
example.answer: The inscriptions are short and there is no bilingual 'key', so the script remains undeciphered.

topics.title: Egypt, Mesopotamia and China: river civilisations

learn.hook: Why did so many early civilisations grow beside great rivers? Think of the Nile, the Tigris and Euphrates, and the Huang He: water, fertile soil and boats!
points: Egypt grew along the Nile. Its yearly floods left fertile mud for farming. Rulers called pharaohs were very powerful; huge pyramids, such as the Great Pyramid of Giza, were built as royal tombs.

Egyptians believed in life after death and preserved bodies by mummification. They wrote in hieroglyphics on papyrus; the Rosetta Stone, carrying the same text in hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek, helped scholars decipher it.

Mesopotamia means 'the land between the rivers' (the Tigris and the Euphrates, in present-day Iraq). Sumerians lived in city-states, built stepped temples called ziggurats and wrote in cuneiform, wedge-shaped marks pressed into clay.
King Hammurabi of Babylon issued a famous code of laws; punishments often depended on a person's social status. The Epic of Gilgamesh is one of the world's oldest stories.

Chinese civilisation grew along the Huang He (Yellow River). Shang rulers used oracle bones, heating bones or shells and reading the cracks, to seek answers about the future. Chinese writing is logographic and the Chinese learned to make silk.

example.q: Think it through: What did the Harappan, Egyptian, Mesopotamian and Chinese civilisations have in common?
steps: All grew in river valleys with water and fertile soil for farming.
Farm surplus supported cities, specialised crafts and trade.
Each developed a form of writing: Harappan script, hieroglyphics, cuneiform and Chinese characters.
Each had organised government and used bronze.
example.answer: River valleys, farming surplus, cities, crafts, trade, writing, organised government and bronze technology.

learn.reallife: Rivers still shape where people live: think of how many Indian cities, such as Varanasi, Patna and Kolkata, stand on the banks of the Ganga or its branches.

topics.title: From jana to janapada to mahajanapada

learn.hook: How did small groups of families, herding cattle and singing hymns, grow into big kingdoms with capitals, armies and taxes? Let us follow the journey along the Ganga plains.
points: Early society was organised in kulas (families or clans) and janas (larger kin-based groups, often called tribes). A jana was led by a raja; the Bharatas were one of the janas mentioned in the Rig Veda.
The raja did not rule alone. Vedic assemblies such as the sabha, the samiti and the vidatha discussed matters and could check the raja's power.

Over time, people of a jana settled in a region, which came to be called a janapada (the land where a jana set foot). Some janapadas grew into larger, powerful states called mahajanapadas. Buddhist and Jaina texts list sixteen mahajanapadas.

Iron tools helped clear forests and plough more land, more crops such as paddy were grown and settlements multiplied in the Ganga plains. Pottery styles of this time include Painted Grey Ware and the glossy Northern Black Polished Ware.

Magadha, in present-day Bihar, became the most powerful mahajanapada. It had fertile land, rivers for transport, iron ore and forests with elephants. Its capitals were Rajagriha (Rajgir) and later Pataliputra (Patna).

example.q: Think it through: Why did Magadha grow stronger than the other mahajanapadas?
steps: The Ganga and Son rivers gave water, fertile soil and easy transport.
Good harvests meant the rulers could collect more taxes.
Nearby iron ore gave tools and weapons; forests supplied elephants for the army.
Capable rulers used these advantages to expand their territory.
example.answer: Fertile land, rivers, iron ore, elephants and ambitious rulers together made Magadha the strongest mahajanapada.

learn.reallife: Rajgir and Patna in Bihar still carry the history of Rajagriha and Pataliputra, and the name 'Bharat' for our country has very old roots.

topics.title: Early states and kingdoms: Mauryas to Cholas

learn.hook: One rock near Girnar in Gujarat carries messages from three different rulers across hundreds of years. Rocks can be history's notice boards!
points: Chandragupta Maurya, guided by Chanakya (Kautilya), defeated the Nanda ruler Dhana Nanda and founded the Mauryan Empire in about 321 BCE, with its capital at Pataliputra.

Ashoka, the most famous Mauryan ruler, was deeply moved by the suffering of the Kalinga war (in present-day Odisha). He then followed Dhamma, a code of compassion, non-violence, tolerance and respect, spread through edicts written mostly in Prakrit in the Brahmi script.
The Junagadh rock inscription near Girnar has records of Ashoka, the Shaka ruler Rudradaman I and the Gupta ruler Skandagupta. It tells how the Sudarshana lake, built in Mauryan times, was repaired.

The Satavahanas ruled the Deccan, while the Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas ruled the far south. The Guptas built a large kingdom in the north; Samudragupta's achievements are praised in the Prayaga inscription composed by his court poet Harishena.

Later powers included the Pallavas of Kanchipuram, the Chalukyas of Badami and the Rashtrakutas. The Palas, Gurjara-Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas fought a long 'tripartite struggle' for control of Kannauj.

example.q: Think it through: Why is the Junagadh rock inscription so valuable to historians?
steps: It carries inscriptions of three rulers from different dynasties: Mauryan, Shaka and Gupta.
So one place shows how power in the region changed over centuries.

topics.title: Ruling a kingdom: ideas of unity and administration

learn.hook: Without phones or trains, how could a king rule lands stretching hundreds of kilometres? Smart ideas, trusted officials and village assemblies!
points: Ancient Indian texts describe dharma, a shared idea of duty, justice and right conduct, which rulers were expected to follow. Texts such as the Mahabharata and Kautilya's Arthashastra discuss the duties of kings.

The ideal of the chakravarti samrat described a ruler whose authority spread across much of the land. Great rituals such as the rajasuya and the ashvamedha were performed to show a ruler's power; names like Bharatavarsha and Jambudvipa expressed the idea of a shared land.
Kings were helped by a council of ministers (mantris) and officials such as the purohita (royal priest), the senapati (army chief) and the samaharta (in charge of collecting revenue).
Kingdoms were divided into provinces, districts and villages. A village headman (gramika) looked after the village, and local bankers, merchants and artisans were sometimes consulted.

Village assemblies managed local matters. Inscriptions at Uthiramerur (Tamil Nadu) from the Chola period describe kudavolai: names written on palm leaves were put in a pot (kudam) and drawn to choose members of village committees.

example.q: Think it through: How is the kudavolai system similar to and different from elections today?
steps: Similar: members of local committees were chosen by a fixed public procedure, not just by the king's order.
Similar: rules described who could be chosen, such as owning land and having good conduct.
Different: names were drawn by lot from a pot, while today voters cast votes for candidates.
Different: today every adult citizen can vote, which is universal adult franchise.
example.answer: Both used rules for choosing local representatives, but kudavolai drew names by lot while modern elections use votes by all adult citizens.

learn.reallife: Today India has states, districts and villages or urban local bodies, and gram panchayats look after local matters, a little like the old village assemblies.

topics.title: Society and economy: varna, jati, guilds and learning

learn.hook: Two thousand years ago, a man donated money to weavers' guilds near Nashik so that the interest would pay for monks' robes. Guilds were like ancient banks!
points: Society was described in terms of four varnas: Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras. Early Vedic texts suggest occupations were flexible: one hymn describes a family with a poet, a physician and a woman who grinds corn.

Over time varna became hereditary, and society also formed many smaller groups called jatis, often linked to occupation, region and marriage within the group. Learned women such as Gargi and Maitreyi are mentioned in the Upanishads.

Merchants and artisans formed guilds called shrenis. They set standards for their work, trained members and even accepted deposits and paid interest. A Nashik cave inscription records an endowment of 3,000 kahapanas deposited with weavers' guilds.

Trade routes such as the Uttarapatha (northern route) and Dakshinapatha (southern route) connected markets. Punch-marked coins were used, and rulers built water works like the Sudarshana lake to support farming.

Students learned in gurukulas, living with the teacher and offering gurudakshina at the end. Great centres of learning included Takshashila, Nalanda and Vikramashila. Tamil Sangam poems and the devotional songs of the Alvars and Nayanars are treasures of this age.

example.q: Think it through: Ushavadata deposited 2,000 kahapanas with one weavers' guild and 1,000 kahapanas with another. What does this tell us about guilds?
steps: The total deposit was 2,000 + 1,000 = 3,000 kahapanas.
The guilds kept the money and paid monthly interest, which was used for the monks living in the caves.
So guilds were trusted enough to hold large sums for a long time.
This shows they worked like banks as well as craft organisations.
example.answer: 3,000 kahapanas in all; guilds acted as financial institutions that accepted deposits and paid interest.

topics.title: Medieval kingdoms: a changing political map

learn.hook: Between 1000 and 1700 CE the map of India kept changing like a giant puzzle: new kingdoms rose, old ones fought back, and some empires grew very large.
points: Around 1000 CE many regional kingdoms ruled India, such as the Cholas in the south and the Chalukyas (Solankis) in Gujarat. Armies from Afghanistan and Central Asia began raiding and later conquering parts of north India.

In 1178, Naiki Devi of the Chalukya kingdom of Gujarat defeated the army of Muhammad Ghuri near Mount Abu. At Tarain, Prithviraj Chauhan defeated Ghuri in 1191, but Ghuri won the second battle of Tarain in 1192.
The Delhi Sultanate began in 1206 with Qutbuddin Aibak and lasted until 1526. Sultans gave officers revenue assignments called iqtas. Many local and regional rulers resisted its expansion.
In the south, the Vijayanagara kingdom was founded in 1336 by Harihara and Bukka. In 1526 Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the first battle of Panipat and founded Mughal rule.

Akbar organised Mughal officials through the mansab system, giving each a rank. Court ceremonies such as the Nauroz festival and jharokha darshan displayed the emperor's power. Rajputs, Ahoms, Marathas, Sikhs and Jats were among those who resisted Mughal power at different times.

example.q: Think it through: The two battles of Tarain were fought in 1191 and 1192. What do their results show about this period?
steps: In 1191 Prithviraj Chauhan won, showing that the invading army could be defeated.
In 1192 Muhammad Ghuri won, which opened the way for the Delhi Sultanate in 1206.
So power changed hands quickly, and the result of a single battle could change history.
It also shows that resistance continued even when a battle was lost, as later regional rulers kept fighting.
example.answer: Power shifted back and forth: the first battle was won by Prithviraj, the second by Ghuri, leading to the Delhi Sultanate.

topics.title: Resistance in the west and north: Rajputs, Marathas and Jats

learn.hook: Picture the rocky Aravalli hills of Mewar and the steep Sahyadri forts of Maharashtra. Rulers here used the land itself as a shield.
points: Rajput kingdoms such as Mewar defended their independence. Rana Sanga of Mewar fought Babur at Khanua in 1527. Akbar's army besieged Chittor in 1567-68, and some other Rajput houses chose alliances with the Mughals instead.

Maharana Pratap of Mewar refused to accept Mughal authority. He fought the Mughal army led by Raja Man Singh of Amber at Haldighati in 1576; the Afghan commander Hakim Khan Sur fought on Pratap's side. Supported by the Bhils and the hilly Aravalli terrain, he continued his struggle for many years.

Shivaji built the idea of Swarajya (self-rule) in Maharashtra. He used hill forts and sea forts, fast-moving cavalry and surprise attacks, and was crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad in 1674. A council of eight ministers, the Ashtapradhan, helped him govern.
The Jats, mostly peasants of the region around Mathura and Agra, rose against heavy Mughal revenue demands under leaders such as Gokula. Their resistance had strong economic causes.
Resistance was not only about battles: it depended on terrain, forts, local support, good organisation and the wish to protect one's own traditions.

example.q: Think it through: Why were hill forts so useful to Shivaji?

topics.title: Resistance in the east and south: the Ahoms and Vijayanagara

learn.hook: On the mighty Brahmaputra, Ahom boats outmanoeuvred a much larger Mughal fleet. Rivers, hills and clever organisation helped the Ahoms stay independent for centuries.
points: The Ahom kingdom of Assam was founded by Sukaphaa in 1228. Ahom rulers governed the Brahmaputra valley for nearly six hundred years, until 1826.
Under the paik system, adult men (paiks) served the state by turns, as soldiers, builders or workers, in return for land. This gave the Ahoms a ready army and workforce.

Ahom commander Lachit Borphukan led the defence against the Mughals. In the battle of Saraighat (1671), fought on the Brahmaputra near Guwahati, the Ahoms defeated the Mughal fleet, using their knowledge of the river and hills.

Vijayanagara (capital near present-day Hampi, on the Tungabhadra river) became a powerful kingdom in the south. Prince Kumara Kampana led a campaign that ended the Sultanate at Madurai; his wife Gangadevi wrote about it in the Sanskrit poem Madhura Vijayam.

Krishnadevaraya was Vijayanagara's most famous ruler and a poet who wrote Amuktamalyada in Telugu. After the battle of Talikota in 1565 against an alliance of Deccan Sultanates, the capital was sacked, but Nayaka rulers carried its traditions forward in the south.

example.q: Think it through: How did geography help the Ahoms defend themselves?
steps: The Brahmaputra is wide, with strong currents and many channels, which the Ahoms knew well.
Their boats and soldiers could move quickly on the river, while outsiders struggled.
Hills and forests around the valley made it hard for a large army to advance.
Combined with the paik system, which gave them organised manpower, this helped them win at Saraighat.
example.answer: Knowledge of the river, hills and forests, together with good organisation, helped the Ahoms resist a larger army.

learn.hook: Resilience means bouncing back. Even in hard times, songs of devotion, festivals, temples, trade and learning kept India's traditions alive and growing.
points: Resistance means opposing a threat or an authority one does not accept; resilience means enduring hardship, adapting and recovering. Both shaped this period.

The Sikh Gurus built a strong community. Guru Arjan Dev compiled the Adi Granth; he was put to death in 1606 on the orders of Emperor Jahangir, and Sikhs remember this as his martyrdom. Guru Hargobind adopted the ideas of miri and piri (worldly and spiritual authority) and built the Akal Takht. Guru Tegh Bahadur was martyred in Delhi in 1675 on Aurangzeb's orders, and Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa in 1699.

Bhakti saints spread devotion in people's own languages: Kabir (nirguna bhakti, devotion to a God without form), Tulsidas (Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi), Surdas (songs on Krishna in Braj), Mirabai, and Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, who led group singing (sankirtan) in Bengal. Sufi saints, living in khanqahs, also taught love and devotion.
Temples destroyed in wars were often rebuilt. The Kashi Vishwanath temple in Varanasi was rebuilt several times; the present temple was built by Ahilyabai Holkar of Indore in 1780.

Economic life continued: merchants used hundis (letters of credit) and sarrafs (money-changers), ports like Surat and Masulipatnam traded overseas, and communities built stepwells, tanks and canals for water.

example.q: Think it through: How did Bhakti saints help traditions survive in difficult times?
steps: They taught that devotion to God mattered more than costly rituals, so anyone could take part.
They composed songs in people's own languages, like Awadhi, Braj and Tamil, which everyone could understand.
Songs could be sung at home and in groups, even when large temples were damaged.
Their poems are still sung today, so the ideas passed down for centuries.
example.answer: By spreading devotion through simple songs in local languages that ordinary people could sing and remember.
